newsitem.title: FRANCE: FORECAST-Mass unemployment to persist in France.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Mass unemployment to persist in France.

text.p: Near-record unemployment will plague France over the next couple of years as economic growth will remain too subdued to make much of a dent in the jobless rate, a Reuter poll of economists showed.
Economists said the main causes of subdued growth and high unemployment were tight budgets and structural rigidities in the job market, both of which act as powerful economic brakes.
The economists' poll predicted that unemployment would remain stuck near all-time highs at least until mid-1998.

The poll forecast an average 1997 unemployment rate of 12.49 percent, slightly higher than the 12.46 percent average rate predicted for 1996. In the second quarter of 1998, economists predicted the rate would drop marginally to 12.23 percent.
Unemployment is currently at 12.6 percent, a record.

The average prediction for year-on-year gross domestic product (GDP) growth in 1997 was 2.2 percent after 1.2 percent this year. By the second quarter of 1998, it is expected to pick up to 2.7 percent year-on-year.
The government is officially forecasting growth of 2.3 percent next year after 1.3 percent this year.
France adopted deficit-cutting budgets in 1996 and 1997 to qualify for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) which aggravated slow growth and high unemployment, economists said.
"What is constraining growth is the long road of tight budget policies," said Francois-Xavier Chauchat, senior fixed-income strategist at Banque Nationale de Paris (BNP).
"Not only France, but Germany and others are going to suffer from subdued growth for the next three or four years," said Nomura International bond strategist Sonja Gibbs.
A Reuter poll of economists released on Wednesday showed that on average they expected Germany's gross domestic product to grow around 2.2 percent in 1997 after 1.2 percent this year.
Economists said it was hard to say if low growth caused high unemployment or vice versa, but they agreed that unemployment was unlikely to improve until the French economy came to life.
"The key is growth," Chauchat said. "Unemployment is a lagging indicator, so even if people see a rebound in the economy, unemployment will not improve. There will be a lag."
Economists also said that France is unlikely to have strong economic growth until it cuts state spending and allows its labour market some flexibility.
"It's job rigidities," Smith Barney international economist Paul Horne said. "State spending is a structural rigidity which limits job creation."

Economists said that monetary union, set to be launched on January 1, 1999, would not provide immediate relief to European economies as it was unlikely to allow interest rates to fall any more or solve the structural problems already present.

But they say that to the extent that EMU forced France to maintain deficit-cutting efforts, it would in the long run stimulate growth and cut unemployment by lowering government spending as a percentage of GDP, thus freeing the economy.
"It (EMU) provides a continuing constraint on the government to cut back the deficit," said Horne.
